props.title: Guess Who's Coming to Dinner

sections.content: Guess Who's Coming to Dinner (1967) stands as a pivotal moment in Hollywood's treatment of interracial relationships. Released just months after the Supreme Court's Loving v. Virginia decision, the film tackled racial prejudice head-on through the story of a white woman (Katharine Houghton) bringing home her Black fiancé (Sidney Poitier) to meet her liberal parents (Spencer Tracy and Katharine Hepburn). Director Stanley Kramer, known for social problem films like The Defiant Ones (1958), deliberately cast Poitier's character as an accomplished doctor to challenge white audiences' racial biases while making the central conflict about marriage rather than dating.

sections.content: The film gains additional poignancy as Spencer Tracy's final performance - he died just 17 days after filming wrapped. His powerful final monologue about love transcending prejudice carries extra weight given his real-life relationship with Katharine Hepburn (their ninth and final film together). While some critics argued the film played it too safe with its upper-middle-class setting and "perfect" Black character, its impact on mainstream audiences was undeniable. In the Heat of the Night (1967), released the same year, took a grittier approach to racial tensions with Poitier as a detective in the Deep South.

The film's influence echoes through later explorations of interracial relationships like Jungle Fever (1991) and Save the Last Dance (2001). Modern films like Get Out (2017) and Loving (2016) continue examining racial dynamics in relationships, though often with sharper critiques of liberal white racism. The dinner table scene format has become iconic, referenced and parodied in countless films addressing family tensions around race, sexuality, and class. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Social Impact

sections.content: Sidney Poitier's role marked a watershed moment for Black representation in Hollywood. While earlier films relegated Black actors to servant roles or racial "problem" narratives, Poitier's Dr. John Prentice was educated, accomplished, and dignified. This portrayal set a template followed by films like Brian's Song (1971) and A Patch of Blue (1965), though some critics later argued this "perfect Negro" characterization created unrealistic expectations.

The film's examination of liberal white racism - parents who support civil rights until it affects their own family - remains startlingly relevant. Modern films like The Big Sick (2017) and Crazy Rich Asians (2018) echo similar themes around interracial relationships and family acceptance, showing how these conversations continue evolving across different cultural contexts.
